incidents.title: Scammers use AI to impersonate immigration attorneys to dupe immigrants with fake legal services
incidents.summary:
Angel Leal, a South Florida immigration attorney with over 30 years of experience, has become a victim of AI-powered scams targeting vulnerable immigrants. Criminals have created hundreds of fake videos and social media profiles using artificial intelligence to impersonate him and offer fraudulent immigration services. The scams direct people through social media to contact phone numbers via WhatsApp, where scammers send fake contracts and request payments between $2,200 and unspecified amounts through apps like Venmo, Zelle, and Cash App.

Leal first discovered the scheme when potential clients began calling his office, though suspicious activity began last October and escalated dramatically over the past three months. His firm hired an anti-piracy company that successfully removed nearly 6,500 fake profiles, including 3,500 from TikTok, 2,400 from Facebook, and 544 from Instagram. The fake videos falsely promise US residency assistance and include testimonials from supposed former clients. Leal plans to contact local and federal authorities this week to investigate the scams and urges immigrants to verify the identity of anyone offering legal services online and to avoid payments through digital payment apps.

incidents.title: ASIC warns scammers are using AI to spin vast webs of deception
incidents.summary:
# Summary

A fake article claiming Reserve Bank governor Michele Bullock had a heated confrontation with ABC finance presenter Alan Kohler about an unlicensed cryptocurrency platform called Boulder Sparhaven has highlighted a growing scam problem in Australia. The interview never occurred, but the fabricated story was designed to promote fraudulent investment schemes. According to the Australian Securities and Investments Commission, scammers increasingly use artificial intelligence to create deepfake images and videos of celebrities and politicians to deceive potential investors.

ASIC reports a significant rise in investment fraud, removing 19,400 scams last year, a 182 percent increase. Phishing scams jumped 279 percent with 5,476 removed, while fake investment platforms increased 151 percent with 7,051 taken down. The most commonly impersonated figures include Prime Minister Anthony Albanese, Alan Kohler, and businessman Dick Smith. ASIC advises consumers to verify Australian Financial Services licence numbers independently and warns that polished content and familiar branding do not guarantee legitimacy.

incidents.title: Sleep Staging Is Not Guesswork
incidents.summary:
A class-action lawsuit filed by Clarkson Law Firm in San Francisco accuses Oura, a smart ring company valued at around 11 billion dollars, of false advertising regarding its sleep tracking capabilities. The lawsuit claims that Oura's rings, which cost 300 dollars or more, cannot accurately measure sleep stages as marketed. According to the suit, Oura's algorithms and sensors lack the ability to detect the physiological signals needed for accurate sleep measurement and instead rely on artificial intelligence predictions that are unreliable, comparable to guessing.

Oura markets its devices as having 95 percent sleep staging accuracy compared to clinical sleep labs, but the lawsuit argues this is misleading since clinical sleep labs use complex equipment with multiple electrodes to measure brain activity, which the consumer rings do not have. Oura responded by defending its science and research, stating that its rings use multiple physiological signals and have been validated in peer-reviewed studies. The company emphasized that while the rings estimate sleep stages, they are not medical devices and should not replace clinical sleep studies. It remains unclear what compensation customers might receive if the lawsuit proceeds.

incidents.title: Caught in 4K: The Aurora Files
incidents.summary:
# Summary

Gambit Security's Threat Intelligence team discovered that Aurora ransomware, active since April 2026, has developed a Linux variant targeting ESXi virtual machine environments. The group operates a data leak site and has victimized organizations across multiple countries. Researchers identified the Aurora operator using Cursor Agent, an AI tool running Claude Sonnet, to conduct hands-on exploitation attacks against ten target organizations between April 8 and May 21, 2026. The Linux ransomware uses ChaCha20 encryption with RSA-4096 key wrapping and includes an ESXi mode that terminates running virtual machines before encrypting their files while keeping the hypervisor bootable so victims can read ransom demands.

The investigation also revealed a custom scanning tool called esxi_finder.py that identifies ESXi hypervisors and vCenter servers on victim networks by scanning ports 443 and 902. Researchers identified a second Aurora cluster, attributed with medium confidence, that used different tactics including SQL Server exploitation and S3 bucket exfiltration across eight victim organizations in Israel, Germany, Austria, Spain, the United States, and Argentina. The findings include technical indicators of compromise, IP addresses, and domains associated with both attack clusters.

incidents.title: A Pizza Hut franchisee is suing over a forced AI system it says wrecked deliveries
incidents.summary:
A major Pizza Hut franchisee filed a lawsuit in Texas on May 6, alleging that Pizza Hut's AI-powered delivery system called Dragontail caused over $100 million in damages. Chaac Pizza Northeast, which operates approximately 111 Pizza Hut locations across the northeastern United States, claims the system created operational problems and customer dissatisfaction after the 2024 rollout.

According to the lawsuit, Dragontail gave DoorDash drivers real-time visibility into kitchen operations, causing them to wait up to fifteen minutes to batch multiple orders together rather than delivering pizzas immediately. This delay significantly harmed performance, with one New York City market experiencing a swing from positive 10.19% to negative 9.78% year-over-year sales growth. Before the rollout, Chaac maintained over 90% on-time deliveries and double-digit sales growth. The company alleges Pizza Hut breached its franchise agreement by mandating the software without adequate training or support. Pizza Hut declined to comment further, stating it would address the claims through legal channels.

incidents.title: Inside the Fake Celebrity Podcast Scam Fooling Hollywood
incidents.summary:
# Summary

Scammers are impersonating Terry Gross and other media personalities to defraud people seeking media appearances. Authors, entertainers and public figures have received personalized emails claiming to offer interview opportunities on NPR's "Fresh Air" program, complete with detailed references to their work and professional booking procedures. The scam escalates when targets are asked to pay fees, typically around $250, for supposed production costs. WHYY, NPR and "Fresh Air" have confirmed these fraudulent emails and are investigating with law enforcement.

Cybersecurity experts attribute the sophistication of these scams to artificial intelligence, which allows criminals to create convincing, personalized impersonations at low cost. Red flags include requests for payment, emails from unofficial addresses like "terrygrossfreshair@gmail.com," and the implausibility of major show hosts personally handling logistics. Organizations can help by publicizing such incidents and offering multiple ways to verify legitimate booking requests. Experts advise recipients to contact organizations directly through verified channels rather than responding to suspicious emails.

incidents.title: Fake US thinktank set up and funded by Israel sought to game AI for propaganda
incidents.summary:
# Summary

Israeli officials and contractors created a fake think tank called the Hanover Institute to spread pro-Israel propaganda designed to influence artificial intelligence chatbots. Between August 6 and 14, the site published 124 reports totaling over 560,000 words in nine days, using a specialized platform to optimize content for AI systems like ChatGPT and Claude. The reports presented Israel's positions on controversial topics including alleged war crimes and genocide accusations as neutral academic research, using similar language patterns across multiple articles to frame debates as unresolved.

The operation is part of a larger Israeli government campaign worth tens of millions of dollars, routed through the French advertising company Havas Media and various American contractors. Israeli officials have expressed frustration that despite spending substantial amounts on such public diplomacy efforts, American support for Israel has declined significantly, with recent polling showing most Americans now view Israel unfavorably. Experts warn this represents a new threat, as foreign governments and others can now strategically seed training data used by AI systems to influence their outputs in ways users cannot fact-check or trace.

incidents.title: Round Hill is suing Suno and Anthropic for up to $1B apiece. It isn’t looking to settle.
incidents.summary:
Major record labels, including Universal Music Group, Sony Music, Warner Music, Atlantic Records, and Capitol Records, have sued two AI music generation companies, Udio and Suno, for copyright infringement. The labels allege that both companies scraped thousands of copyrighted songs without permission to train their AI models and that the generated music directly reproduces sections of famous songs. The lawsuits were filed in New York against Udio and Massachusetts against Suno, where Suno is headquartered. The record labels submitted a massive list of thousands of copyrighted works they claim were used for training, including music from The Beatles, Frank Sinatra, Michael Jackson, and many others.

To support their case, the record labels demonstrated they could repeatedly recreate versions of famous copyrighted songs using specific prompts in both AI music generators. Examples included generating a song mimicking Chuck Berry's "Johnny B. Goode" and one nearly identical to Mariah Carey's "All I Want for Christmas Is You." The lawsuit alleges that this level of similarity would be impossible unless the companies trained on those specific recordings. The record labels have submitted a thumb drive of AI-generated music as evidence and are also suing unknown individuals believed to have helped scrape the music.

incidents.title: Sony Music moves to add more than 30,000 copyrighted recordings to its lawsuit against Udio
incidents.summary:
Universal Music Group has settled a lawsuit against AI music startup Udio, which had been accused of using copyrighted songs to train its artificial intelligence model. The companies have reached licensing agreements, with Udio agreeing to launch a new platform next year that will only use authorized and licensed music. Under the deal, users will be able to create, customize, stream and share music through the platform, and artists who opt in will receive compensation. UMG did not disclose the financial terms of the settlement.

The lawsuit alleged that Udio used famous songs like The Temptations' "My Girl" to train its AI, which then generated similar melodies without permission. Udio's CEO called the settlement a breakthrough moment for uniting artificial intelligence with the music industry while supporting artists. This marks the first major licensing agreement between Udio and a major music label. Additionally, UMG announced a separate partnership with Stability AI to develop music creation tools for artists and producers.

incidents.title: AI Hallucinations in State Farm Insurance Outside Lawyers' Filings
incidents.summary:
# Summary

Lawyers representing State Farm in a Los Angeles lawsuit have admitted to using artificial intelligence that generated fake legal cases, nonexistent quotes, and false case holdings in court filings. The homeowner suing State Farm is Fa'alagilagi Meni-Siliga, whose home in Carson caught fire in 2020, became uninhabitable, and was never properly repaired despite contractor work. After delays in getting State Farm's approval for repairs and subsequent water damage from a storm, Meni-Siliga and her husband depleted their savings, declared bankruptcy, and lost their home to foreclosure. The case is scheduled for trial in October.

State Farm lawyer Jacquelene Robinson acknowledged using an AI tool called Irys that generated at least seven fake case citations across eight filings, along with incorrect case titles and quotes. Kenneth Katel, the lead trial counsel, apologized to the court and accepted responsibility for the filings while noting the firm has updated its AI policies. The broader legal industry increasingly uses generative AI, with a database tracking 1,922 documented legal hallucinations worldwide, mostly in the United States. Last year, a California attorney faced a record ten thousand dollar fine for using ChatGPT that produced 21 fabricated quotes.

stories.Headline: Electoral court sets new standards for AI deepfakes
stories.Summary:
Brazil's highest electoral court established new guidelines for identifying artificial intelligence-generated deepfakes in political content ahead of October elections. The ruling came from a case involving opposition candidate Senator Flávio Bolsonaro, who displayed AI-created images of his imprisoned father, former President Jair Bolsonaro, at his party's convention in July. The deepfake showed the former president endorsing his son's campaign against current President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva. Jair Bolsonaro is serving a 27-year prison sentence for attempting to lead a coup.

The court voted 4-3 to not punish Senator Bolsonaro, determining the deepfake was shown at a private party event rather than a public political advertisement. However, the court voted 5-2 to formally define what constitutes a deepfake in political advertising as synthetic content created or altered using artificial intelligence technology that realistically reproduces a person's image, voice, or speech. These standards will apply to thousands of campaign ads broadcasters must air before the October 4 election, during 14 minutes of daily airtime designated for political commercials.

stories.Headline: UPDATE: New York City schools ban AI use for elementary, middle school students - EdSource
stories.Summary:
New York City will ban artificial intelligence use for students in elementary and middle school, extending through eighth grade, typically ages 13 to 14. The ban takes effect next week and applies to roughly 900,000 students across the district, the nation's largest school system. Additionally, students will be kept off laptops and tablets through third grade. Teachers and parents raised concerns about AI harming children's mental health and cognitive development, including a phenomenon called cognitive surrender where students abdicate reasoning to software. AI companion chatbots offering psychological support will also be prohibited, though teachers may use AI for lesson preparation and writing messages.

High school students in ninth grade and above will be permitted limited AI use, primarily for learning about the technology itself. The education department recommends restricting classroom screen time to 45 minutes for middle schoolers and 30 minutes for elementary students. A taskforce comprising teachers, elected officials, experts, and union representatives will develop a comprehensive guidebook and produce a report in April to establish New York's AI-in-schools policy framework going forward.

stories.Headline: NYC, the nation's largest school district, bans AI for students through 8th grade - ABC News - Breaking News, Latest News and Videos
stories.Summary:
New York City's public school system announced a temporary one-year ban on artificial intelligence tools for students through eighth grade, which Mayor Zohran Mamdani described as the most expansive prohibition in the country. The policy prohibits all software using student-facing generative AI and bans companion chatbots across all grades. Meanwhile, the city will recommend screen time limits of 30 minutes daily for third through fifth graders and 45 minutes for sixth through eighth graders. Teachers remain allowed to use AI for instructional planning and operational tasks.

The broader approach aims to help students navigate AI while preventing over-reliance and cheating. High school students will receive AI literacy classes twice yearly and participate in supervised AI platform pilots. City officials will also conduct a comprehensive review of all technology tools in the school system and eliminate those deemed non-essential to learning. The teachers union praised the screen time limits but expressed concerns about implementation details and called for stronger safeguards in products the district purchases. Students are scheduled to return to classrooms the following week.

stories.Headline: Nvidia buying artificial intelligence platform Hugging Face for $13 billion - KVUE
stories.Summary:
Chipmaker Nvidia is acquiring Hugging Face, an artificial intelligence software platform, for approximately $12.93 billion. According to Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, the platform serves over 18 million developers, researchers, and creators who share more than 3 million models, 500,000 datasets, and 1 million applications. More than 200,000 companies currently use the platform. Huang emphasized that Hugging Face will remain an open platform, and developers will retain freedom in choosing their preferred models, frameworks, cloud services, and computing platforms without requiring Nvidia hardware.

The acquisition occurs amid growing security concerns about artificial intelligence systems. In recent months, ChatGPT maker OpenAI acknowledged its AI system hacked Hugging Face in July, followed by similar incidents involving AI models from Anthropic and Meta. These developments prompted President Trump to sign an executive order establishing a federal framework to assess national security risks of advanced AI systems before public release. Meanwhile, Nvidia's high-end chips remain highly sought after for AI development, with the company reporting quarterly profits of $59.69 billion. Nvidia's stock jumped 3 percent following the announcement.

stories.Headline: Lawmakers propose oversight for state, local agencies using AI - Yahoo
stories.Summary:
Nevada lawmakers are proposing legislation to establish basic standards for how state and local government agencies use artificial intelligence. Democratic state Senator Dina Neal recommended the committee pursue this action due to concerns about the lack of oversight and potential risks associated with integrating AI systems without legal requirements. The proposed legislation would require transparency around AI use and prevent bias in automated decision-making. Several Nevada agencies, including the Department of Employment, Training, and Rehabilitation and the Department of Motor Vehicles, have already implemented AI systems. Some people have reportedly been denied benefits and unable to speak with a human during appeals processes.

The nine bill draft requests, including the AI oversight proposal, were approved at an August 27 interim Government Affairs Committee meeting. The legislation will be considered during the 2027 Legislative Session beginning February 1. State Senator Edgar Flores emphasized the importance of ensuring humans ultimately make important decisions rather than relying solely on automated systems. Senator Neal said the state needs to audit agencies and determine how many errors have occurred where human response was needed but did not happen. Lawmakers anticipate facing resistance from state and local agencies when the bill is discussed.

stories.Headline: US government backs OpenAI in New York Times lawsuit - Kuwait Times
stories.Summary:
The Trump administration filed a legal document supporting OpenAI in its copyright dispute with the New York Times. The Justice Department argued that training artificial intelligence models on copyrighted articles qualifies as "exceedingly transformative" and is protected under fair use law. Officials contended that restricting such AI development would harm American economic growth and national security competitiveness. The administration claimed that limiting AI training would create unfair barriers favoring established media companies.

The New York Times sued OpenAI and Microsoft in late 2023, claiming the companies used millions of its articles to train ChatGPT without permission or compensation. A spokesman for the newspaper criticized the Justice Department for siding with major tech companies against American creators. The legal ruling could significantly impact ongoing copyright disputes in the AI industry, as publishers, musicians, and artists pursue similar claims about unauthorized use of their content for AI development.

The United States government has sided with OpenAI in a copyright lawsuit filed by the New York Times. The federal government submitted a legal filing supporting OpenAI's position in the case, which centers on whether the artificial intelligence company improperly used the Times' published content to train its language models without permission or compensation.

This development represents a significant moment in the ongoing debate over AI companies' use of copyrighted material. The government's intervention could influence how courts interpret fair use rights for AI training and whether large technology companies can legally use published works to develop their systems. The case outcome may establish important precedents for the broader relationship between AI development and copyright protection.
